subject: TTFT & streaming requirements — post-call recap and next steps
messages:
From: Aditya Rao <aditya.rao@redwoodinference.com>
To: Jenna Ortiz <jenna.ortiz@finserve.com>, Carlos Mendez <carlos.mendez@finserve.com>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwoodinference.com>
Date: Wed, 25 Feb 2026 16:10:00 -0800
Subject: TTFT & streaming requirements — post-call recap and next steps

Thanks again for the demo today — great conversation. Quick recap of the performance/streaming items we discussed and proposed next steps so we have alignment:

What we captured
- TTFT (time-to-first-token) target: <= 150 ms p95 on your baseline test case (you mentioned aiming for ~120 ms in ideal conditions).
- Streaming: primary option is SSE or WebSocket for server-sent streaming; you noted WebSocket is preferred by your frontend team but SSE could be acceptable as fallback.
- Chunk cadence: target chunk frequency ~150–300 ms (or ~1–3 KB per chunk) to keep UX responsive without excessive framing overhead.
- Throughput / concurrency: expected steady-state ~200 reqs/sec with spikes to ~1,000 reqs/sec; concurrently active streaming sessions ~400–500 with up to 800 during peak events.
- Latency SLOs by route: interactive chat route p95 <= 150 ms TTFT, batch generation routes p95 <= 400 ms.

Proposed next steps
1) Confirm the baseline payload (examples attached in Drive link) we should use to run the TTFT test — Jenna/Carlos can you confirm which prompt + context size you want us to test?
2) Decide streaming protocol for the test: WebSocket preferred? If yes, we’ll run the WebSocket streaming test first and then an SSE run as a fallback comparison.
3) Schedule a joint engineering run with your infra/FE team — 60–90 minutes to run synthetic load and capture traces.
4) We’ll share an SLO template and load test plan (attached) and a link to the test harness.

Attachments: slo-template.pdf (SLO + test plan stub)

Open questions
- Do you have any connection limits / corporate proxy constraints that would force us to prefer SSE or chunked polling?
- Any authentication constraints (mTLS or specific token TTLs) we should provision for the test environment?

I’ll start lining up engineering availability next week if you confirm a target window. Thanks — A

--

From: Jenna Ortiz <jenna.ortiz@finserve.com>

Date: Thu, 26 Feb 2026 09:05:00 -0800
Subject: Re: TTFT & streaming requirements — post-call recap and next steps

Thanks Aditya — helpful recap. A few clarifications from our side:

- TTFT: we’d like to target p95 <= 120 ms for the chat UI (this is aggressive but critical for our UX).
- Streaming protocol: our frontend team prefers WebSocket for lower overhead and more control over connection lifecycle; SSE is acceptable if WebSocket proves unreliable behind our corporate proxies.
- Chunk cadence: aim for ~150–250 ms cadence on chat messages; smaller chunks are fine as long as TTFT target is met.
- Concurrency: steady-state ~250 active streams with peaks up to 800. Throughput ~300 rps steady, peaks 1k rps.

We have a corporate proxy that terminates long-lived SSE connections in some regions — will need to work with infra if SSE is the only route. For authentication, we prefer short-lived JWTs (1–2 min TTL) issued by our auth service; mTLS is not required for the PoC.

Attached: finserve-network-diagram.pdf (shows proxy behavior and regional egress points).

Next steps from our side: we can provide the canonical prompt + payload and a sandbox account for testing. We’re flexible for the engineering run next Tue/Wed afternoon PST.

-Jenna
Product Manager, FinServe Inc.
jenna.ortiz@finserve.com
From: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwoodinference.com>

Date: Thu, 26 Feb 2026 11:30:00 -0800
Subject: Re: TTFT & streaming requirements — post-call recap and next steps

Quick engineering note / proposed test approach:

- We’ll validate TTFT in two phases: 1) single-client microbench to measure platform baseline (no network variability), 2) distributed load test from multiple regions to emulate proxy and egress behavior (matches your network diagram).
- WebSocket test first (since it’s your preferred), then SSE fallback. For WebSocket we’ll measure: handshake time, first-binary/frame latency, and chunk arrival cadence. For SSE we’ll measure connection stability behind your proxies (we’ll instrument for proxy disconnects and reconnect cadence).
- Chunk size/cadence: the test harness can be configured to emit chunks every 100–300 ms and vary payload sizes (512B, 1KB, 3KB) to see TTFT and UI render tradeoffs.
- Concurrency: we’ll target a ramp to 1k rps with a steady plateau at 300 rps and 500–800 concurrent streams. We’ll capture per-token latency histograms and system-level metrics (GPU utilization, KV cache hit rates, batching stats).

Request from FinServe for the test
- Please confirm the canonical prompt(s) and average context size (tokens). That will determine model selection/quantization profile.
- Provide an auth token TTL expectation for the sandbox (JWT TTL 1–2 min noted by Jenna is fine).

I’ll prepare a short load-test checklist and a link to the harness (internal doc) — sharing the public link to the test plan now: https://redwood.cloud/loads/FS-2026-045-test-plan

We’ll sync engineering presence for the session — Aditya, I can join the Wed window if we target 11:00–13:00 PST.

-Marissa
Senior Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference

1) Jenna/Carlos: please drop the canonical prompt(s) and average context size into the Drive link by EOD Monday (we’ll use the sandbox credentials you provide).
2) Aditya/Marissa: we’ll schedule the engineering run for Wed 11:00–12:30 PST (Marissa to lead load test, I’ll run the client-side harness).
3) I’ll update the attached SLO template with the p95 = 120 ms TTFT for the chat route and share the updated PDF before the run.
4) Post-run: we’ll share a short findings doc (latency breakdown, throughput curve, recommended config: batching, KV cache, and model quantization profile) within 48 hours.
